# AML evidence packet — draft v1

This curated input is not a comprehensive review. Every method receives the same UTF-8 file. Summaries are original paraphrases. Bibliographic metadata and abstracts were checked through the public NCBI ID converter and PubMed EFetch on 2026-10-05. Selected studies predate 2025. Co-Scientist's validated candidates and generated proposals are not input or the only correct answers.

## Research question

Propose one mechanistically specific AML drug-repurposing hypothesis using a drug approved for a different indication. Specify the biological context, supported premises and speculative bridges, selectivity and translational limitations, and a discriminating preclinical validation strategy with a falsifying outcome. State the original indication and distinguish verified facts from prior knowledge that needs checking. Do not present an established AML regimen as a new repurposing discovery. This adapts the Co-Scientist objective rather than reproducing a private original prompt.

## S1 — A leukemia-stem-cell metabolic dependency

Lagadinou et al. (2013), *BCL-2 inhibition targets oxidative phosphorylation and selectively eradicates quiescent human leukemia stem cells*. Cell Stem Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.stem.2012.12.013`; PMID: `23333149`; PMCID: `PMC3595363`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23333149/).

Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens frequently had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. This motivates investigating specific dependencies and selectivity. It does not establish that an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor has an acceptable therapeutic window or works across every AML context.

## S2 — Resistant cells are not necessarily the same stem-cell population

Farge et al. (2017), *Chemotherapy-Resistant Human Acute Myeloid Leukemia Cells Are Not Enriched for Leukemic Stem Cells but Require Oxidative Metabolism*. Cancer Discovery. DOI: `10.1158/2159-8290.CD-16-0441`; PMID: `28416471`; PMCID: `PMC5501738`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28416471/).

Residual cells in cytarabine-treated models were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells. They displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties, including mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features. Altering that state changed treatment response in the studied settings. This cautions against equating all residual disease with the ROS-low population in S1. These model findings do not establish clinical efficacy of a new compound.

## S3 — An established mechanistic comparator

Pollyea et al. (2018), *Venetoclax with azacitidine disrupts energy metabolism and targets leukemia stem cells in patients with acute myeloid leukemia*. Nature Medicine. DOI: `10.1038/s41591-018-0233-1`; PMID: `30420752`; PMCID: `PMC7001730`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30420752/).

The report connected venetoclax–azacitidine treatment to changes in leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects, using patient-associated observations and experimental follow-up. It provides an established comparator. Repeating this combination is not a new repurposing proposal. The findings cannot be transferred directly to another drug or treated as universal randomized comparative efficacy evidence.

## S4 — Differentiation as a distinct outcome

Sykes et al. (2016), *Inhibition of Dihydroorotate Dehydrogenase Overcomes Differentiation Blockade in Acute Myeloid Leukemia*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2016.08.057`; PMID: `27641501`; PMCID: `PMC7360335`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27641501/).

DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the investigated models. This connects metabolism with differentiation and supplies an alternative to nonspecific cell killing. It does not establish that every approved drug affecting this pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity.

## Evidence boundaries

- Specify context and endpoint; distinguish bulk-cell effects, stem-cell effects, and differentiation.
- Approval, original indication, exposure and selectivity facts outside these summaries need explicit verification. Label recollections as unverified prior knowledge.
- Include normal-cell and mechanistic comparators; a pathway link alone is insufficient evidence of efficacy.
- State what would disconfirm the proposed drug–mechanism–context relationship.
- Absence from Co-Scientist's reported positive candidates is not an incorrect-answer label.


Proposed answer (the answer to evaluate):
Teriflunomide at multiple-sclerosis-relevant exposure induces DHODH-dependent myeloid differentiation in differentiation-arrested acute myeloid leukemia blasts relative to normal CD34-positive progenitors

This hypothesis proposes that teriflunomide will drive myeloid differentiation of differentiation-arrested human AML blasts by inhibiting dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH). The original indication (multiple sclerosis), approval status, the relationship of teriflunomide to leflunomide, and clinically achieved plasma concentrations are unverified prior knowledge. They require confirmation from regulatory labels and pharmacokinetic sources before they are treated as facts.

Supported premises come from the supplied summaries. [S4] reports that DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the models investigated. That evidence links a metabolic enzyme to release of a differentiation block and identifies differentiation as an outcome distinct from nonspecific cell killing. [S4] leaves unresolved whether every approved drug that affects this pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity.

The intended biological context is primary AML blasts that show morphologic and immunophenotypic differentiation arrest. Bulk viability, differentiation, and leukemia-stem-cell readouts are separate endpoints. Neighboring evidence sets the comparators. [S1] reports that functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens frequently had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2, and that BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. [S2] reports that residual cells in cytarabine-treated models were not consistently enriched for immature quiescent leukemia stem cells; they displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties, including mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features, and altering that state changed treatment response in the studied settings. [S3] connects venetoclax with azacitidine to changes in leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects. Venetoclax-azacitidine is an established comparator. This proposal uses a different drug and asks first whether differentiation occurs in differentiation-arrested blasts.

Speculative bridges. Bridge A: at exposures used for multiple sclerosis, teriflunomide inhibits DHODH in AML blasts. Drug identity and exposure remain unverified prior knowledge. Bridge B: differentiation-arrested patient blasts share the pyrimidine-linked dependency observed in the experimental systems of [S4], so this approved agent engages the same differentiation program. Bridge C: matched normal CD34-positive progenitors tolerate those concentrations with less differentiation pressure and less loss of clonogenicity than the leukemic blasts. Bridge D: the differentiation effect is separable from oxidative-phosphorylation suppression after BCL-2 inhibition [S1], [S3] and from the fatty-acid-oxidation-associated state of cytarabine-residual cells [S2]. A pathway link alone is insufficient evidence of efficacy.

Alternative explanations should be tested in the same experiment. Mature-marker enrichment can follow selective death of immature blasts with persistence of a pre-existing mature fraction. If uridine salvage replenishes pyrimidines, phenotypes that appear only at high concentration may reflect off-target kinase or mitochondrial activity. Cytarabine-residual cells of the kind described in [S2] may continue to rely on oxidative metabolism whether or not blast differentiation changes. A decrease in ROS-low quiescent cells would constitute a distinct stem-cell claim aligned with the dependency class in [S1], and it would need its own positive and negative controls. AML genotype and salvage capacity are free to dominate and are unspecified here.

The discriminating preclinical test uses paired cultures of pre-specified differentiation-arrested primary AML blasts and normal CD34-positive hematopoietic cells. Teriflunomide is applied across a range anchored to verified steady-state exposure. Arms are vehicle, uridine rescue, a tool DHODH inhibitor as the class-mechanism comparator motivated by [S4], and a BCL-2 inhibitor analyzed only as the oxidative-phosphorylation and leukemia-stem-cell comparator motivated by [S1] and [S3]. Three endpoint families are scored separately: myeloid differentiation by morphology, CD11b and CD14 or other lineage-appropriate markers, and colony maturation; bulk viability and apoptosis; and, where cell numbers allow, frequency and function of ROS-low quiescent leukemia-initiating cells. A cytarabine-residual arm, built in the spirit of the models summarized by [S2], receives the same three scores so that residual oxidative disease is a separate context.

Falsifying observation: the drug-mechanism-context claim fails if exposure-anchored teriflunomide leaves AML differentiation endpoints indistinguishable from vehicle, if a differentiation increase remains after uridine rescue, or if normal CD34-positive progenitors show equal or greater differentiation or clonogenic loss at those concentrations. Failure to reduce ROS-low leukemia-initiating cells falsifies a stem-cell-eradication extension and leaves the differentiation claim dependent on the differentiation endpoints alone. Absence of activity in the cytarabine-residual arm falsifies extension to that population [S2] and limits any supported context to differentiation-arrested blasts.

Limitations. Selectivity in patients, unbound marrow exposure, and clinical benefit are unshown. Serum binding and medium uridine can distort the apparent window. [S1] withholds any assumption that mitochondrial stress implies a therapeutic index. [S2] keeps residual disease distinct from the ROS-low stem-cell population. [S3] does not transfer efficacy from venetoclax-azacitidine to teriflunomide. Genotype heterogeneity is untested. Among the supplied sources, [S4] supports the DHODH-differentiation premise only; no supplied source tests teriflunomide in AML.

Ranked proposal:
Teriflunomide at multiple-sclerosis-relevant exposure induces DHODH-dependent myeloid differentiation in differentiation-arrested acute myeloid leukemia blasts relative to normal CD34-positive progenitors
